what_its_for: Vincristine is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat certain types of cancer, including leukemia, lymphoma, and other cancers. It works by stopping cancer cells from growing and dividing.
how_to_take: Vincristine is given as an injection directly into a vein (IV infusion) by a nurse or doctor in a hospital or clinic setting. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Each treatment session may take only a few minutes or up to an hour depending on the type of vincristine you receive. Never allow this medicine to be given as a spinal injection — this is extremely dangerous. Remind your healthcare team every time that this medicine is for IV use ONLY.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your body size, type of cancer, and overall health. Doses are usually given once a week as part of a larger chemotherapy schedule. Always follow the schedule your cancer care team gives you. Do not ask for extra doses or change the schedule on your own.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given in a clinic or hospital, your healthcare team will schedule your appointments carefully. If you miss or need to reschedule an appointment, call your cancer care team right away. Do not try to make up a missed treatment on your own — your doctor needs to decide the safest next step for you.
storage: Vincristine is stored and handled by healthcare professionals in a clinical setting. You do not need to store this medicine at home. If you are ever given any supplies related to your treatment to take home, keep them out of reach of children and pets, and follow any specific instructions given to you by your care team.
what_to_avoid: Avoid getting vaccinations (shots) without asking your doctor first, especially live vaccines like the flu nasal spray or shingles vaccine, as they can be dangerous while you are on chemotherapy. Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections, since vincristine can lower your ability to fight germs. Avoid alcohol unless your doctor says it is okay. Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements you take, as many can interact with vincristine. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel weak, dizzy, or have numbness in your hands or feet.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: severe constipation or no bowel movement for 3 or more days; numbness, tingling, burning, or weakness in your hands or feet; severe jaw or muscle pain; difficulty walking or loss of balance; signs of infection such as fever over 100.4°F (38°C), chills, or cough; difficulty breathing; unusual bruising or bleeding; extreme tiredness or weakness; or if you cannot eat or drink due to nausea or mouth sores. These may be signs of serious side effects that need immediate attention.
when_it_works: Vincristine starts working right away at the cellular level, but you may not see or feel results immediately. Your doctor will monitor your progress through blood tests and other exams. It may take several weeks or months of treatment before you notice improvement. It is very important to keep all your scheduled treatment and follow-up appointments even if you feel well.
special_populations: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects such as nerve problems (numbness or weakness) and constipation, so extra monitoring may be needed. Children can also receive vincristine, and doses are carefully calculated based on body size. People with liver disease may need dose adjustments because vincristine is processed by the liver. Pregnant women should not receive vincristine as it can harm the unborn baby — use effective birth control during treatment and discuss this with your doctor. Breastfeeding is not recommended while on vincristine. People with a pre-existing nerve condition (neuropathy) should inform their doctor before starting treatment.
